groups.h: The map of this topic — four algorithms, two jobs
points: You must know **two searching algorithms** — linear search and binary search — which *find* an item in a list, and **two sorting algorithms** — bubble sort and merge sort — which put a list *in order*. Every question in this topic is about one of these four, so knowing each one's mechanism, best/worst case and ideal use covers everything.

**Golden rule #1:** binary search **only works on a sorted list**. Hand it unsorted data and it confidently throws away the half containing your target. When a question shows a jumbled list and asks *'why is binary search not appropriate?'* the one-mark answer is simply: *the list is not sorted.*

**Golden rule #2 (the scale rule):** for **large** data, the clever algorithms (binary search, merge sort) win massively; for **tiny** lists or one-off jobs, the simple ones (linear search, bubble sort) are perfectly fine and easier to write. Almost every 'which would you choose?' question is answered by checking: *sorted or not? large or small? searched once or repeatedly?*

Exam questions come in three flavours: **describe** how an algorithm works, **apply** it to a given list (trace it), or **compare** two algorithms and justify a choice. Prepare a rehearsed answer for each flavour and this chapter becomes very predictable.

groups.h: Linear search — checking the queue one by one
points: **How it works:** start at the **first** item and compare each item **in turn** with the target, stopping when you find it or run out of list. It is exactly how you'd look for your name on an unsorted register: top to bottom, one line at a time.
Its quiet superpower: it needs **no preparation** — the list can be in any order, sorted or shuffled. That's the advantage to quote whenever linear search is the right choice.

**Best case:** the target is the **first** item → 1 comparison. **Worst case:** the target is **last or absent** → all *n* items checked. **Average for a successful search:** about half the list, n/2, because the target is equally likely to be anywhere.
The cost problem: on 1,000,000 records, an unlucky search means 1,000,000 comparisons. Fine for a 10-item shopping list; hopeless for a national database searched thousands of times a day.

**Describe-it answer (3 marks, rehearse it):** *start at the first item (1); compare each item in turn with the target (1); stop when the target is found or the end of the list is reached, meaning it is not present (1).*

groups.h: Binary search — split the phone book
points: **The idea:** in a *sorted* list, one comparison with the **middle** item tells you which half the target must be in — so you can throw the other half away. Repeat on the surviving half, halving and halving until you hit the target or run out of list. It's exactly how you find a name in a phone book: open the middle, decide left or right, repeat.

**The mechanical version (this is the 4-mark describe answer):** (1) examine the middle item, found with `mid = (first + last) DIV 2`; (2) if it equals the target — done; (3) if the target is **greater**, discard the lower half by setting `first = mid + 1`; if **smaller**, discard the upper half with `last = mid - 1`; (4) repeat until found, or until `first > last`, which means the search area is empty and the target is **not in the list**.

**Best case:** the target *is* the middle item — found in **one** comparison. **Worst case:** the target is absent (or found only when one item remains) — about **log₂(n)** comparisons. This exact best/worst question appears on real papers for 2 easy marks.

Feel the power of halving: 1,000 items → at most ~10 comparisons (because 2¹⁰ = 1,024). 1,000,000 items → ~20. And **doubling the list adds just ONE comparison**. That single sentence — *each comparison halves the search area, so doubling the data adds only one step* — is the 'why is it efficient?' answer.

**Trace technique for exams:** write `first`, `last`, `mid` as columns. Each round: compute mid with DIV, note the *value* examined, then move first or last. The examiner wants the **sequence of items examined** (e.g. 17, 31, 25) — practise until producing it takes under a minute.

**Why sorted is non-negotiable:** the whole trick is 'the target must be in this half *because the list is ordered*'. Unsorted data breaks that guarantee, so the discarded half might contain the target — the search can fail even though the item is right there.

groups.h: Linear vs binary — how to answer every comparison question
points: Binary search's case: on large sorted lists it is dramatically faster — 1,000 items: ≤10 comparisons vs up to 1,000; 1,000,000 items: ~20 vs up to 1,000,000. Quote actual numbers; comparisons with numbers hit the top of the mark scheme.

Linear search's case (yes, it has one — 'binary is always better' is FALSE): (1) it works on **unsorted** data with zero preparation; (2) it's **simpler to implement**; (3) on **tiny** lists it's just as fast; (4) if the data is searched only **once**, sorting it first costs more than it saves; (5) if the target happens to be item 1, linear finds it in one comparison while binary still takes several.

The sort-then-search decision: unsorted data searched **once** → linear, straight in. Searched **many times** → sort once (merge sort), then binary-search cheaply forever after — the sorting cost is repaid across thousands of fast lookups. This trade-off is a favourite 3–6 mark discussion.

A neat efficiency middle ground the exam likes: a linear search on a *sorted* list can **stop early** the moment it meets a value bigger than the target — the target can't appear later in ordered data.

groups.h: Bubble sort — swapping neighbours until calm
points: **How it works:** compare items 1 and 2 — swap if out of order. Then items 2 and 3, then 3 and 4… to the end. That full sweep is **one pass**. Keep making passes until a **complete pass makes no swaps** — no swaps means every neighbouring pair is in order, which means the whole list is sorted. That swap-free pass is *how the algorithm knows it's finished* (a 2-mark question in its own right).

After pass 1, the **largest** value has been carried step-by-step to the **end** — it 'bubbles up' like air in water, which is where the name comes from. Each further pass locks the next-largest into place, so after k passes the last k positions are guaranteed final.

**Trace method that never drops marks:** rewrite the whole list after every swap, working pair by pair. Don't swap equal values. The exam's favourite ask is *'show the list after the first pass'* — with `5 2 4 1`: swap 5,2 → 2 5 4 1; swap 5,4 → 2 4 5 1; swap 5,1 → 2 4 1 5. Answer: **2 4 1 5**, three swaps.

The numbers examiners ask for: one pass over *n* items makes **n − 1 comparisons**; a reverse-ordered list (worst case) needs n − 1 swap-making passes plus one checking pass, with (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1 total swaps; an **already-sorted** list needs just **one pass, zero swaps** — bubble sort's one genuine strength.

The swap itself needs a **temp** variable: `temp ← A, A ← B, B ← temp`. Without temp, the first assignment overwrites a value and both boxes end up holding the same number — a standard find-the-error question.
groups.hook: ** *biggest bubbles to the back; no swaps = sorted.*

groups.h: Merge sort — divide till single, merge till whole
points: **The 4-mark description (rehearse verbatim):** (1) repeatedly **divide** the list in half (2) until every sub-list holds **one item** — and a one-item list is automatically sorted; (3) then repeatedly **merge pairs** of sub-lists, comparing their front items and always taking the **smaller** first, so each merged list comes out in order; (4) keep merging until a single sorted list remains.

**Merging two sorted lists** is the engine: compare the two front items, move the smaller into the result, repeat; when one list runs empty, copy the rest of the other straight across. Merging [2,7] and [3,9]: 2 vs 3 → 2; 7 vs 3 → 3; 7 vs 9 → 7; copy 9 → [2,3,7,9]. Practise this until it's mechanical — it's the part traces test.

Full worked shape for 8 items [7,3,9,1,6,2,8,5]: divide → [7,3,9,1][6,2,8,5] → [7,3][9,1][6,2][8,5] → singles. Merge level 1 → [3,7][1,9][2,6][5,8]; level 2 → [1,3,7,9][2,5,6,8]; level 3 → [1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9]. Notice the symmetry: 3 levels down, 3 levels up (because 2³ = 8).

Merge sort always does its full pattern of divides and merges **regardless of the data's starting order** — it has no early finish on sorted data (unlike bubble). The upside: its performance is **predictable**; the downside: no best-case bonus.

groups.h: Bubble vs merge — which sort, when, and why
points: **Merge sort wins on large lists, by miles.** Its divide-and-merge workload grows gently as lists grow, while bubble sort's repeated passes explode — sorting 250,000 leaderboard scores with bubble sort means billions of comparisons. Any scenario with big data (leaderboards, databases, logs) → merge sort, and say *'far fewer comparisons on large lists'*.

**Bubble sort's honest advantages** (needed for balanced answers): (1) much **simpler** to understand and implement; (2) sorts **in place** — merge sort needs **extra memory** to hold the merged lists; (3) finishes in **one pass** on an already/nearly sorted list, which merge sort cannot exploit.

The standard 2-marker: *merge sort for 100,000 race times (efficiency at scale); bubble sort for a hand of 6 cards (simplicity, tiny data)*. Match the algorithm to the **size** in the scenario and give the size as your reason.
Both sorts always produce the **same final order** — they differ in speed and memory, never in the result.

**Comparison-count cheat sheet to quote:** linear worst = n; bubble pass = n − 1 comparisons; binary worst ≈ log₂(n) → 1,000 items ≈ 10, 1,000,000 ≈ 20, and doubling the list adds one; merge sort of 8 items = 3 divide levels + 3 merge levels.

groups.h: Exam technique — traces and 'which algorithm?' questions
points: Bubble trace answers: write the **whole list after each pass** (that's what the mark scheme checks), count swaps pair-by-pair, and remember equal values don't swap. If asked whether a given list 'could be the state after one pass', check one thing first: **is the largest value at the end?** If not, impossible.

Binary trace answers: give the **items examined in order** (the midpoints), using `mid = (first + last) DIV 2` whenever positions are given. For not-found traces, show the moment **first > last** — that's the mark for 'how does it know the search failed'.

Best/worst-case questions want the **scenario**, not just a number: *best = target is the middle item (binary) / first item (linear); worst = target absent or found last.* Add the comparison count if marks allow.

'Which algorithm and why' questions: anchor every reason in the scenario's three facts — **sorted? large? searched repeatedly?** *'Binary search, because the list is sorted and large (30,000 items), so each lookup needs about 15 comparisons instead of up to 30,000'* is a full-mark sentence.

For 6-mark discussions, structure as: option A's strengths with numbers → option B's strengths → a one-line recommendation tied to the scenario ('lookups vastly outnumber re-sorts, so sort once with merge and binary-search thereafter'). Balanced + applied + concluded = top band.
